blocks.content: In Abstraction, PaymentProcessor was written as an interface without you dwelling on the mechanics. Here, interfaces get the full spotlight, especially the one thing they can do that inheritance cannot: let a single class guarantee multiple unrelated capabilities at once.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

An interface is a pure contract, a set of method signatures with no implementation and no state, that any class can promise to fulfill using the implements keyword. Unlike extending a class, a single class can implement many interfaces at once.

Java only allows a class to extend one superclass, but real objects often need multiple, unrelated capabilities. A Duck needs to fly AND swim, but "flying" and "swimming" are not naturally an IS-A relationship with each other, they are independent abilities. Interfaces let Duck promise both without forcing an awkward single-inheritance hierarchy.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884659251-935512510.png
blocks.alt: The USB standard implemented independently by a mouse, a keyboard and a printer

blocks.content: A mouse, a keyboard, and a printer are completely unrelated devices, yet all three can plug into the same USB port because they all honor the same USB standard. USB does not care what the device actually is, only that it fulfills the contract.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884660918-471311826.png
blocks.alt: The electrical socket standard implemented independently by a lamp, a charger and a fan

blocks.content: An electrical socket works the same way: a lamp, a phone charger, and a fan share nothing in common as devices, but all three can plug into the exact same socket standard. The socket is the contract, each device is free to implement "being powered" however it needs to.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884662363-511827121.png
blocks.alt: Single inheritance blocking Duck from extending two classes, solved by implementing two interfaces instead

blocks.content: Interfaces solve the problem of needing multiple, independent capabilities on one class when single inheritance would otherwise force an awkward choice. Duck cannot extend both a Bird class and a Fish class, but it can freely implement both a Flyable interface and a Swimmable interface.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: An interface is a reference type that defines a set of abstract methods (a contract) with no implementation, which any class can agree to fulfill using the implements keyword. A single class may implement multiple interfaces, unlike extending multiple superclasses.
4. Key Terminology

["Interface: a pure contract of method signatures, with no implementation or state.","implements keyword: declares that a class fulfills an interface’s contract.","Multiple interface implementation: one class implementing more than one interface at the same time.","Default method: a method inside an interface that DOES have a body, giving implementing classes a fallback if they do not override it.","Functional interface: an interface with exactly one abstract method, usable with lambda expressions."]
items: Interface: a pure contract of method signatures, with no implementation or state.
implements keyword: declares that a class fulfills an interface’s contract.
Multiple interface implementation: one class implementing more than one interface at the same time.
Default method: a method inside an interface that DOES have a body, giving implementing classes a fallback if they do not override it.
Functional interface: an interface with exactly one abstract method, usable with lambda expressions.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884663863-628126545.png
blocks.alt: Duck implementing both the Flyable and Swimmable interfaces at the same time

blocks.content: Duck sits at the bottom of two completely separate contracts. It is not "a Flyable that happens to also be a Swimmable," it simply promises to fulfill both contracts independently, and provides its own concrete fly() and swim() to do so.

7. Code Breakdown

["interface Flyable { void fly(); } and interface Swimmable { void swim(); } are two completely independent contracts, neither knows the other exists.","class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable promises to fulfill both contracts, and must provide a real fly() and swim(), or the code will not compile.","Flyable flyer = duck; a Duck can be referenced through EITHER interface type, code that only cares about flying can depend on Flyable and stay completely unaware that Duck can also swim.","flyer.fly(); still calls Duck’s actual fly() implementation, the interface reference does not change which code runs, only what the reference is allowed to see."]
items: interface Flyable { void fly(); } and interface Swimmable { void swim(); } are two completely independent contracts, neither knows the other exists.
class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable promises to fulfill both contracts, and must provide a real fly() and swim(), or the code will not compile.
Flyable flyer = duck; a Duck can be referenced through EITHER interface type, code that only cares about flying can depend on Flyable and stay completely unaware that Duck can also swim.
flyer.fly(); still calls Duck’s actual fly() implementation, the interface reference does not change which code runs, only what the reference is allowed to see.

9. Behind the Scenes (Default Method Conflicts)
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884666830-530777268.png
blocks.alt: Two interfaces both providing a default greet method, forcing the implementing class to resolve the conflict itself

blocks.content: Java interfaces can include default methods, methods with an actual body, giving implementing classes a ready-made fallback. This creates one tricky edge case: if a class implements two interfaces that both define a default method with the exact same signature, the compiler cannot guess which one you mean. It refuses to compile until the implementing class overrides that method itself and explicitly picks (or combines) the behavior it wants.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884668265-21498183.png
blocks.alt: Independent interface capabilities combined on a single class across e-commerce, banking, social and gaming domains

blocks.content: ["E-commerce: an Order can implement both Refundable and Shippable, two independent capabilities with nothing to do with each other conceptually.","Banking: a Transaction can implement both Auditable and Taxable at once.","Social Media: a Post can implement both Likeable and Shareable at once.","Gaming: a GameObject can implement both Damageable and Collectible at once, a treasure chest that can also be destroyed, for example."]
items: E-commerce: an Order can implement both Refundable and Shippable, two independent capabilities with nothing to do with each other conceptually.
Banking: a Transaction can implement both Auditable and Taxable at once.
Social Media: a Post can implement both Likeable and Shareable at once.
Gaming: a GameObject can implement both Damageable and Collectible at once, a treasure chest that can also be destroyed, for example.

blocks.content: This same pattern shows up constantly in the Java standard library itself:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884669711-996298968.png
blocks.alt: A custom class implementing both the standard Comparable and Serializable interfaces

blocks.content: It is completely normal for one class to implement Comparable (so it can be sorted) AND Serializable (so it can be saved to a file or sent over a network) at the same time, two totally unrelated capabilities, combined freely because interfaces do not compete with each other the way superclasses would.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["A class can implement as many interfaces as it genuinely needs, unlike single class inheritance.","An interface cannot hold instance state (fields), only method contracts and constants."],["Interfaces decouple \"what a class can do\" from \"what a class actually is.\"","Too many tiny, overlapping interfaces can fragment a design and make it harder to see the full picture."],["Default methods let an interface evolve (adding new methods) without breaking every existing implementer.","Conflicting default methods from two interfaces require explicit, manual resolution."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Cramming unrelated methods into one giant interface, when several small, focused interfaces would model the capabilities more honestly.","Forgetting that interface fields are implicitly public static final constants, not regular mutable state.","Assuming an interface can have a constructor or instance fields the way a class can, it cannot.","Implementing an interface just because a method happens to be useful, rather than because the class genuinely fulfills that contract’s intent."]
items: Cramming unrelated methods into one giant interface, when several small, focused interfaces would model the capabilities more honestly.
Forgetting that interface fields are implicitly public static final constants, not regular mutable state.
Assuming an interface can have a constructor or instance fields the way a class can, it cannot.
Implementing an interface just because a method happens to be useful, rather than because the class genuinely fulfills that contract’s intent.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Keep interfaces small and focused on one capability, Flyable should only be about flying.","Name interfaces after capabilities (Flyable, Comparable) so their intent is obvious at a glance.","Prefer implementing multiple small interfaces over one large interface with methods some implementers do not really need.","Use default methods sparingly, mainly for genuinely optional, backward-compatible behavior, not as a substitute for a shared abstract class."]
items: Keep interfaces small and focused on one capability, Flyable should only be about flying.
Name interfaces after capabilities (Flyable, Comparable) so their intent is obvious at a glance.
Prefer implementing multiple small interfaces over one large interface with methods some implementers do not really need.
Use default methods sparingly, mainly for genuinely optional, backward-compatible behavior, not as a substitute for a shared abstract class.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["An interface is a pure contract, method signatures with no implementation, that a class fulfills using implements.","A class can implement multiple interfaces at once, unlike extending multiple superclasses.","Default methods give interfaces an implementation fallback, but conflicting defaults from two interfaces must be resolved manually.","Interfaces decouple capability (what a class can do) from identity (what a class fundamentally is).","Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large interface trying to describe everything."]
items: An interface is a pure contract, method signatures with no implementation, that a class fulfills using implements.
A class can implement multiple interfaces at once, unlike extending multiple superclasses.
Default methods give interfaces an implementation fallback, but conflicting defaults from two interfaces must be resolved manually.
Interfaces decouple capability (what a class can do) from identity (what a class fundamentally is).
Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large interface trying to describe everything.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked "why use an interface instead of an abstract class," the fastest correct answer is: a class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class, so interfaces are the tool for granting multiple, independent capabilities that do not share a natural IS-A hierarchy with each other.
